source: International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) - Rice Knowledge Bank / USDA-ARS Dale Bumpers National Rice Research Center
title: Rice Blast Disease (Magnaporthe oryzae, syn. Pyricularia oryzae, Ascomycota Magnaporthaceae)
content: Rice blast, caused by the heterothallic haploid ascomycete filamentous fungus Magnaporthe oryzae B.C. Couch (anamorphic stage Pyricularia oryzae Cavara; class Sordariomycetes, order Magnaporthales, family Magnaporthaceae) is the single most destructive and economically costly fungal disease of cultivated rice (Oryza sativa L.) worldwide. The rice-Magnaporthe pathosystem is also the most extensively studied model molecular pathosystem in modern fungal plant pathology (the 'drosophila' of plant pathology) because of the genetic tractability of both host and pathogen, the complete genome sequences of both organisms, and the enormous agricultural significance of the disease. Rice blast occurs in all 85+ rice-growing countries of the world, across all rice ecosystems (irrigated lowland, rainfed lowland, upland, deep-water, floating, mangrove tidal wetland, and temperate irrigated rice). Annual global rice yield losses from blast are conservatively estimated at 10-30% of total global production, equivalent to approximately 30-100 million tonnes of milled rice (2023 production year data), enough food to feed 60-180 million people annually. In individual localized epidemics, yield losses of 50-100% are routinely recorded in highly susceptible cultivars under severe blast-favorable weather (prolonged periods of cool, humid, overcast, dewy nights with intermittent rain and moderate day temperatures 24-28 C). Beyond direct yield losses, rice blast also significantly reduces head rice yield and milling recovery (by 10-30% due to chalky and pecky grain kernels infected with panicle blast), and causes major economic losses in high-value hybrid rice, scented jasmine, and basmati rice production due to quality-grade downgrading of grain with blast lesions. The taxonomic genus Pyricularia contains approximately 50+ species that collectively infect > 100 species in the family Poaceae (grass family) including wheat (Triticum aestivum, infected by the closely related M. oryzae Triticum lineage MoT - wheat blast, which emerged in Brazil in 1985 and in Bangladesh in 2016, now a major threat to global food security), finger millet (Eleusine coracana), foxtail millet (Setaria italica), maize (Zea mays, weakly), barley (Hordeum vulgare), oats (Avena sativa), perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne), tall fescue (Festuca arundinacea), St. Augustine grass (Stenotaphrum secundatum), crabgrass (Digitaria sanguinalis), signalgrass (Brachiaria), and many wild grasses. The M. oryzae species complex (the 'Pyricularia oryzae / P. grisea species complex' sensu lato) is subdivided into genetically distinct, host-specialized formae speciales (pathotypes) with very limited cross-infectivity between host genera: M. oryzae Oryza pathotype (MoO) infects only cultivated and wild Oryza species and is the causal agent of classical rice blast; MoT (Triticum) = wheat blast; MoE (Eleusine) = finger millet blast; MoS (Setaria) = foxtail millet blast; MoL (Lolium) = gray leaf spot of ryegrass and turfgrasses; each is reproductively isolated from the others via female sterility and host specialization. Rice blast can infect all above-ground parts of the rice plant at any growth stage, giving rise to a spectrum of disease syndromes named after the affected plant part: (1) Seedling blast (pyricularia seedling blight): infection of 1-4 leaf-stage rice seedlings in the nursery seedbed; causes small, water-soaked, gray-green, diamond-shaped lesions that expand rapidly, causing seedling wilt, dieback, and death of up to 80% of nursery seedlings in severe cases. (2) Leaf blast (the most commonly observed syndrome, 'classical blast'): individual lesions on fully expanded rice leaves are characteristically diamond-shaped (lanceolate, spindle-shaped, ellipsoidal) with pointed (acuminate) tips and narrow ends, 5-40 mm long x 3-15 mm wide, with three distinct color zones visible: a central flattened, grayish-white to off-white necrotic sporulating zone (where the fungus is actively producing conidia under humid conditions), a wide middle zone of reddish-brown or brown necrotic tissue, and a narrow, sharp, yellowish chlorotic halo at the lesion margin (the yellow halo is produced by the host-specific Magnaporthe phytotoxin pyricularin and secondary phytotoxic metabolites tenuazonic acid, pyriculol, and picolinic acid). Lesions produced on highly susceptible rice cultivars under high inoculum pressure may remain small, circular to oval, uniformly dark brown to black, non-sporulating (hypersensitive Type 1 reaction); on intermediate cultivars, typical sporulating diamond lesions (Type 4-5) develop; on highly resistant cultivars carrying a matching major Pi resistance gene, only tiny (0.5-1 mm), dark brown, non-sporulating, hypersensitive necrotic flecks (Type 2-3 reaction) develop and the fungus is halted by a hypersensitive response (HR) programmed cell death within 24-48 hours. (3) Collar rot (collar blast): infection occurs at the junction (collar) of the leaf sheath and leaf blade; causes a brown to dark gray necrotic girdling lesion that kills the entire leaf blade ('flag leaf collar blast' immediately before heading is the most damaging collar symptom because the flag leaf contributes approximately 40-50% of total photosynthate translocated to the filling rice grain). (4) Node blast: infection occurs on rice stem nodes (the swollen jointed regions of the culm where leaves and tillers attach); causes dark brown to black, sunken, girdling necrotic lesions that can completely destroy the vascular system of the culm, causing the entire portion of the tiller above the infected node to dry up and die prematurely, resulting in white, unfilled 'blank' panicles (node blast is frequently confused with stem rot caused by Sclerotium oryzae, and with false smut Ustilaginoidea virens-infected panicles). (5) Leaf sheath blast: elongated dark brown lesions on outer leaf sheaths; usually of minor economic importance except when it progresses to the culm node. (6) Panicle blast / Neck blast / Neck rot (the most economically damaging syndrome, because it directly affects yield and grain quality): infection occurs on the panicle base or 'neck' (the uppermost 5-10 cm of the rice culm immediately below the panicle, also called the 'peduncle') within 5-20 days after heading (flowering, anthesis). Neck blast lesions are initially brown to dark purple-black, water-soaked, girdling the panicle neck; as the lesion expands it turns grayish-black, shrivels, and causes the entire panicle above the neck to turn white, die, and dry up completely (the characteristic 'white head' or 'blank head' symptom) 2-3 weeks before normal grain ripening. The grains in a neck-blighted panicle are completely unfilled, empty, light-weight, chalky, sterile, and worthless for either human consumption or seed purposes. (7) Panicle branch blast and grain blast: individual spikelets, panicle branches (rachillae and primary/secondary panicle branches), and glumes can be infected after heading, producing small dark brown necrotic lesions on glumes and panicle branch nodes; individual infected grains are small, chalky, discolored ('pecky rice'), have reduced milling yield, and are frequently contaminated with mycotoxins (tenuazonic acid, alternariol, beauvericin, moniliformin - regulated by many countries under food safety mycotoxin limits). Magnaporthe oryzae overwinters (survives between rice cropping seasons) primarily in three forms: (1) as mycelium, conidia, and perithecia (sexual fruiting bodies) in infected rice crop residue (rice stubble, straw, and panicle debris) left on the soil surface after harvest; rice straw and stubble is the most important primary inoculum source in temperate and subtropical rice-growing areas where rice is planted once per year; in double-cropped rice systems with a late fall / winter fallow period, crop residue inoculum drives the early-season nursery and leaf blast epidemics. (2) as seedborne inoculum: M. oryzae can survive internally as mycelium in the endosperm, embryo, and palea/lemma of infected rice seed at rates of 0.1-15%, and externally as conidia on the seed hull surface; seedborne inoculum is the primary mechanism of international long-distance spread and the most important source of initial leaf blast infection in commercial rice nurseries and seedbeds. (3) on alternate gramineous weed hosts: many wild grass species (Echinochloa crus-galli barnyardgrass, Leptochloa chinensis sprangletop, Digitaria ciliaris crabgrass, Brachiaria mutica para grass, Cynodon dactylon bermudagrass, Oryza barthii wild African rice, O. rufipogon common wild rice, O. officinalis complex wild rice) are naturally infected by rice-pathotype strains of M. oryzae and serve as a perennial 'green bridge' inoculum reservoir in tropical rice areas with no winter fallow. The asexual polycyclic disease cycle of rice blast is extremely well characterized and proceeds as follows: under conditions of high relative humidity (RH > 92%), warm temperatures (24-28 C), and darkness (6-12 hours of nighttime dew), enormous numbers of pyriform (pear-shaped), 2-septate, hyaline to pale olivaceous, asexual conidia (20-35 x 8-15 um; the characteristic 'Pyricularia' conidium shape is highly diagnostic) are produced sympodially on slender, erect, 3-5 septate, geniculate (knee-like bent) simple conidiophores (100-400 x 3-5 um) emerging through stomata and epidermal cells of sporulating leaf and panicle blast lesions. A single leaf blast lesion can produce 2,000-40,000 conidia per night for up to 20 successive nights under optimal conditions. Conidia are dispersed primarily by wind (turbulent atmospheric boundary-layer flow can carry conidia 5-50 km from a source field; typical within-field dispersal is via splash droplets of rain and irrigation water and via wind gusts of 10-500 m). After deposition on a rice leaf surface, each conidium adheres tightly via a mucilaginous spore-tip mucilage released from the apical cell of the conidium upon hydration. Within 30-60 minutes under humid conditions, each conidium germinates by producing a polarized germ tube (10-20 um in length) from one of its two end cells; the germ tube ceases polar growth, hooks, and swells at its tip to form a highly specialized, dome-shaped, melanin-pigmented infection structure called an appressorium (10-20 um diameter). The appressorium is the defining infection structure of M. oryzae: it accumulates massive concentrations of glycerol (3.0-3.5 M, osmotic pressure ~ 8 MPa = 80 atmospheres) via gluconeogenesis from storage lipid and glycogen reserves in the conidium, and uses this enormous turgor pressure to mechanically punch through the rice plant cuticle and epidermal cell wall via a thin penetration peg produced from the appressorial pore; this process of mechanical penetration does not require enzymatic cell-wall degradation (though cutinase and cellulase enzymes play a secondary role). The entire process of conidial germination, appressorium formation, melanization, turgor generation, and penetration takes approximately 16-24 hours on a susceptible cultivar. After penetration, the fungus grows as thin primary invasive hyphae inside the first penetrated rice epidermal cell; it then switches to bulbous, lobed, biotrophic invasive hyphae (IH) that invaginate the host plasma membrane (the 'extrainvasive hyphal membrane' EIHM compartment) and move from cell to cell via plasmodesmatal connections using a specialized structure called the biotrophic interfacial complex (BIC), which secretes protein effectors (Avr = avirulence gene products, and 100+ other cytoplasmic and apoplastic effectors) into the host cytoplasm and apoplast to suppress host PAMP-triggered (PTI) and effector-triggered (ETI) immunity. Approximately 4-7 days after penetration, the fungus switches from biotrophy to necrotrophy, the host cells die, and the characteristic necrotic blast lesion becomes visible; 1-2 days later, conidiophores emerge from the lesion surface and produce a new crop of conidia to start the next infection cycle. Under ideal conditions, the entire latent period (infection to new conidial production) is only 5-7 days, and multiple repeated polycyclic secondary cycles drive explosive logarithmic epidemic spread through a rice crop within 3-4 weeks. Sexual reproduction (teleomorph stage: formation of dark, ostiolate, flask-shaped perithecia, 200-400 um diameter, on the surface of overwintered rice straw) occurs readily in the laboratory and in some field locations when fertile strains of opposite A1 / A2 MAT mating types are paired; perithecia contain 8-spored asci with fusiform ascospores. The role of sexual ascospores in the field epidemiology of rice blast remains poorly studied but is presumed to be most important in areas with mild winters and abundant straw residue, and as a source of genetic recombination generating new virulent pathotype races. Host genetic resistance (Pi = resistance genes) is the most effective, economical, and environmentally sound method for controlling rice blast. Two classes of genetic resistance exist in rice: (1) Major, dominant, race-specific resistance genes (R genes / Pi genes, > 100 named Pi loci characterized to date, ~ 35 cloned and sequenced) are typically nucleotide-binding site leucine-rich repeat (NBS-LRR) proteins that recognize specific matching Magnaporthe avirulence (Avr) effector proteins secreted by the pathogen into the host cell, triggering a strong hypersensitive response (HR) programmed cell death that halts infection at the penetration stage within 24 hours (the 'gene-for-gene' model of Flor, 1956). Pi genes (e.g., Piz-t, Pi9, Pi2, Pi54, Pita, Pi1, Pi-ta, Pik, Pib, Pi33, Pi5, Pi56) have been widely deployed in rice breeding programs worldwide and are responsible for the majority of rice blast control in modern high-yielding cultivars. The major disadvantage of monogenic Pi-gene deployment is that strong directional selection on the pathogen population drives rapid evolution of virulent mutant M. oryzae races that lose or modify the matching Avr effector gene, typically overcoming a newly deployed major Pi gene within only 3-7 years of widespread commercial use. (2) Quantitative, partial, horizontal, field (polygenic) resistance (QR, also called quantitative trait locus QTL-mediated resistance, adult-plant resistance APR, panicle blast resistance Pbr) is mediated by the combined action of many loci with small to moderate individual phenotypic effects; QR is generally race-nonspecific, does not trigger a hypersensitive response, reduces the rate of lesion development, expansion, and sporulation without preventing infection completely, and is considered to be considerably more durable over time than major-gene vertical resistance. The modern strategy for durable rice blast resistance, mandated by IRRI, the CGIAR Rice CRP, and national rice breeding programs globally, is to 'pyramid' (stack) multiple (3-6+) different major Pi genes with complementary and broad-spectrum race specificities together with high levels of polygenic panicle blast QR using marker-assisted backcrossing (MABC), genomic selection (GS), and speed breeding. Commercially important blast-resistant modern rice varieties released by IRRI and national programs include: 'IR50404-57-2-2-3', 'IR64', 'IR72', 'IR8', 'Swarna-Sub1 + Pi9 pyramids', 'Ciherang-Sub1 + Pi2/Pi54', 'BRRI dhan28, dhan29, dhan57' (Bangladesh), 'Rasi', 'BPT 5204 Improved + Pi1/Pi2/Pi54' (India), 'Teqing', '9311 + Pigm' (China; the Pigm gene from the Chinese landrace 'Gumei 4' is a famous broad-spectrum blast resistance locus used widely in Chinese hybrid rice breeding), 'Reizihao', 'Tetep' (classic broad-spectrum resistance donor landrace). Management of rice blast requires an integrated program combining resistance, seed health, cultural practices, forecasting models, and judicious fungicide use. (1) Seed health and seed treatment: plant only M. oryzae-indexed, certified rice seed produced in blast-free arid seed-increase zones; treat seed before planting with a 12-hour soak in carbendazim 0.1% + mancozeb 0.2%, or with tricyclazole 0.05%, hot water seed treatment at 52-54 C for 10-15 minutes, or with dry-dressing fungicides (carboxin + thiram, tebuconazole + trifloxystrobin, fluquinconazole) to eliminate both internal and external seedborne inoculum; this practice alone reduces nursery seedling blast incidence by 70-90%. (2) Cultural practices: (a) balanced fertilization: avoid excessive nitrogen (N) application (application of more than 120-150 kg N/ha on susceptible cultivars dramatically increases rice blast severity because lush, N-fertilized tissue has reduced silicon content and lower resistance); split N fertilizer into 3-4 split applications (basal, active tillering, panicle initiation, heading) rather than applying it all at once. Silicon (Si) fertilization (200-400 kg calcium silicate slag / wollastonite per hectare) is a particularly effective cultural practice against rice blast: absorbed silicon deposits in the epidermal cell walls as silica phytoliths, physically impeding appressorial penetration; Si-deficient soils (low available Si, typical of highly weathered oxisols and ultisols in tropical lowland rice areas) can see rice blast severity reductions of 50-75% following calcium silicate amendment. (b) water management: in irrigated lowland rice systems, maintain a continuous 5-8 cm floodwater depth from transplanting through panicle initiation; intermittent drying and wetting (non-flooded 'aerobic rice' and alternate wetting-and-drying AWD water-saving irrigation) significantly increases rice blast severity compared to continuous flooding because of enhanced N mineralization producing N-lush growth. (c) crop residue management: in temperate single-crop rice areas, collect, remove, burn, incorporate deeply by moldboard plowing, or compost (hot compost > 55 C for 3 days) all rice straw and stubble residue after harvest to reduce overwintering inoculum levels in the field by 60-85%. (d) planting density: avoid over-seeding rates and excessive transplant plant densities that promote humid, poorly ventilated microclimates in the crop canopy. (e) planting date and crop duration: adjust planting date to avoid the most blast-conducive cool, humid, dewy periods of the year during the vulnerable seedling and heading/flowering growth stages (the two stages when rice is most susceptible); early-maturing varieties can often 'escape' severe late-season panicle blast if planted sufficiently early. (f) eliminate gramineous weed hosts (barnyardgrass, sprangletop, crabgrass, wild Oryza spp.) from within rice fields and field borders to prevent green-bridge inoculum carryover between rice crops. (3) Forecasting and disease warning models (BLASTCAST, RICEPEST, EPIRICE, IRRI BlastCast, WUR Epiblast, China National Rice Blast Forecasting System) predict regional blast risk using meteorological data (temperature, RH, rainfall, dew duration hours, sunshine hours, wind speed), historical blast survey data, cropping calendar, and inoculum potential; these models are used operationally in many countries (Japan, Korea, Philippines, India, China, USA) to schedule fungicide applications only when economic thresholds of infection risk are exceeded, reducing fungicide use by 30-50% compared to calendar-based spray programs. (4) Chemical fungicide programs: in temperate rice-growing regions and in hybrid rice and high-quality basmati / jasmine rice production with high blast risk, fungicides represent a standard component of the rice IPM program. The most effective and widely used rice blast fungicide classes (based on IRRI, USDA, JIRCAS, and CAAS trial data) are: (a) Melanin biosynthesis inhibitors (MBI, the classic rice blast-specific fungicide class): MBI-D = inhibitors of scytalone dehydratase, MBI-R = inhibitors of 1,3,8-trihydroxynaphthalene (T3HN) reductase; they act by preventing the formation of melanin in appressorial cell walls, without which the appressorium cannot generate turgor pressure and is unable to penetrate the rice plant. Tricyclazole (75% WP, 300 g ai/ha; the most famous, most widely used rice blast fungicide globally since the 1970s) is the prototypical MBI with excellent protectant + 3-5 day curative kickback activity, very low risk of resistance, long residual activity (21-30 days), and extremely low mammalian and aquatic toxicity. Pyroquilon and phthalide are older MBI fungicides still used in Japan and Korea. (b) FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, difenoconazole, propiconazole, prothioconazole, epoxiconazole, mefentrifluconazole): broad-spectrum systemic fungicides with good protectant + curative activity against leaf, node, and panicle blast; always tank-mixed with multi-site partner to prevent DMI resistance. (c) FRAC 11 QoI / strobilurins (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, picoxystrobin, coumoxystrobin, enoxastrobin): excellent protectant + translaminar systemic activity, good grain yield-enhancing 'greening' effect even in the absence of disease; QoI resistance (Cyt b G143A and F129L) in M. oryzae is reported from Japan, Korea, and parts of China, so QoIs are always tank-mixed with tricyclazole or multi-site and alternated with non-QoI modes of action. (d) FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, isofetamid, benzovindiflupyr, pydiflumetofen, pyrimorph variants): newer broad-spectrum protectant + mild systemic activity; rice blast SDHI use is expanding rapidly. (e) FRAC M3 multi-site contact protectants (mancozeb, maneb, zineb, chlorothalonil, propineb): backbone protectant materials, always used as tank-mix partners; zero resistance risk. (f) FRAC 9+12 cyprodinil + fludioxonil, FRAC 40 CAAs (dimethomorph, mandipropamid - weak activity on rice blast), FRAC P07 phosphonates. All rice blast fungicides are generally applied as 2-4 foliar sprays per crop: spray 1 at maximum tillering (for leaf blast control), spray 2 at late boot / panicle initiation stage, spray 3 at 50-70% heading (for panicle blast, the most critical timing to protect yield and grain quality), spray 4 at 10-15 days after heading (late panicle blast). For paddy lowland rice, fungicides are typically applied by high-clearance self-propelled ground sprayers or by aerial fixed-wing / drone application in the large rice production areas of the USA, Brazil, Argentina, and Australia. (5) Biological control (BCAs): commercial formulations of Bacillus subtilis B-916, B. amyloliquefaciens FZB42, Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf-1, Streptomyces griseoviridis, Trichoderma harzianum, T. viride, Beauveria bassiana (note: B. bassiana is an entomopathogen but also shows endophytic blast-antagonist activity in rice), Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast, and a chitinolytic Streptomyces lydicus strain WYEC 108 have all shown 40-70% rice blast reduction in small-plot IRRI trials; biological control is most effective as a nursery seedbed drench combined with 1-2 foliar sprays at early tillering, and is a key component of organic rice production. (6) Host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) and RNA interference (RNAi)-based transgenic and spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS) technologies are under advanced development at IRRI, CAAS, the Sainsbury Laboratory, and the John Innes Centre: SIGS-based topical spray application of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) targeting essential M. oryzae pathogenicity genes (MoABC1, MoSLN1, MoMC69, MoTUB2, MoDES1, appressorial melanin biosynthesis genes) onto rice leaves has provided 80-95% blast control in greenhouse trials and represents a potential future fungicide-free control technology. Finally, the 2016 wheat blast (MoT) pandemic emergence in Bangladesh and the subsequent spread to India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Zambia has dramatically re-emphasized the importance of rigorous global pathogen surveillance, coordinated international quarantine measures, M. oryzae pathotype monitoring programs (the IRRI Global Blast Monitoring Network GBMN), and accelerated resistance breeding and cisgenic/transgenic approaches for all M. oryzae-affected cereal crops.
